newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq has no more banned weapons, Aziz says.
newsitem.headline: Iraq has no more banned weapons, Aziz says.

text.p: Deputy Prime Minister Tareq Aziz said on Wednesday Iraq was stripped of materials and weapons banned under the 1991 Gulf War ceasefire.

Aziz sent a letter to the chairman of the U.N. Security Council in response to the half-yearly report to the council presented by Rolf Ekeus, head of the U.N. Special Commmission (UNSCOM) in charge of Iraqi disarmament, on April 12.
"There are no banned weapons or their components or means to produce them and there are no banned activities in Iraq," Aziz said in the letter carried by the official Iraqi News Agency.
Ekeus accused Iraq of concealing small but significant quantities of banned weapons.
Aziz dismissed the charge as "mere suspicions and suppositions which cannot be certified".
UNSCOM confirmation that Iraq has destoryed its weapons of mass destruction is a key conditions for the removal of the remaining curbs on Iraqi oil exports.
Iraq is currently exporting limited amounts of oil under a U.N. plan to ease the imapct of sweeping economic sanctions imposed for its 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

Ekeus also said Iraq was obstructing U.N. arms monitoring activities as well as helicopter flights by his arms inspectors. He urged Baghdad to make a political decision "once and for all" on its ambitions to retain and acquire dangerous arms.
Aziz said UNSCOM had 332 Iraqi sites under constant surveillance and that its export-import mechanism to ensure no banned materials entered Iraq was in full operation.
The UNSCOM report neglected Iraqi progress in the annihilation of its weapons and focused on issues which the two sides could easily solve by working together, he said.
He said "serious progress" was made in the past six months to close files on chemical weapons and the ballistic missiles with ranges beyond 150 km (90 miles).
Aziz said he had agreed with Ekeus on steps to close the biological warfare file, still the thorniest issue in relations with UNSCOM.
He said Ekeus's inspectors had carried out 550 missions in Iraq in the past six months and the biological experts had subjected 86 Iraqi installations to constant monitoring.
Obstruction of monitoring activities by Iraq were not the norm but exceptions, carried out by individuals who did not receive clear-cut instructions, he said.
"Iraq's decision to give up its weapons of mass destruction and not possess them in the future is an obvious decision," Aziz said.
